4 Study of O2-IMS K8s interface
4.1 Context

The background for this study arises from the increasing adopIon of cloud-naIve network funcIons and their impact on infrastructure management systems. Cloud-naIve principles advocate for declaraIve-based management for network funcIons, wherein the desired end state is described, rather than specifying the sequence of steps to achieve that state. The shiC towards declaraIve models has not been fully explored for infrastructure management services within the context of the O2 interface.

As of specificaIon v04.00, O2-IMS interfaces follow an imperaIve model approach for infrastructure management. This approach does not enable direct cloud naIve integraIon with Kubernetes which is a prominent container orchestrator widely used in the industry.

The study's findings are expected to provide insights into the feasibility and benefits of adopIng a declaraIve K8s API approach for the O2-IMS interface. This analysis will assist WG6 in making informed choices regarding the evoluIon of O2-IMS ecosystem. By understanding the impact and potenIal modificaIons, the study aims to accelerate the adopIon of O2-IMS and leverage industry best pracIces.
4.2 Objectives

The main objecIve of the present Technical Report is to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the O2-IMS interface with a focus on exploring the feasibility, drawback and benefits of adopIng a declaraIve K8s API approach.
To achieve this goal, the study is structured around the following specific objects:

• DeclaraIve K8s API approach
  • O2-IMS services analysis
  • Proposal for O2-IMS K8s interface support
  • Impact on WG6 SpecificaIons and Use Cases
4.3 Declarative K8s API approach
4.3.1 Kubernetes Object Management techniques
As defined in the Kubernetes Object Management [2] documentaIon, three management techniques exist:
• Imperative commands

• o "A user operates directly on live objects in a cluster. The user provides operaIons to the kubectl command as arguments or flags."
  • o "This is the recommended way to run a one-off task in a cluster; it operates directly on live objects and provides no history of previous configurations."
  • Imperative object configuration
    • o "The kubectl command specifies the operation (create, replace, etc.), optional flags, and at least one file name. The file specified contains a full definition of the object in YAML or JSON format."
  • Declarative object configuration
    • o "A user operates on object configuration files stored locally; however, the user does not define the operations to be taken on the files. Create, update, and delete operations are automatically detected per object by kubectl. This enables working on directories, where different operations might be needed for different objects."
The Kubernetes documentaIon exemplifies and defines advantage and disadvantage for each of these techniques.
4.3.2 Declarative object management benefits

DeclaraIve Kubernetes (K8s) API is one of the fundamental concepts that Kubernetes is built upon. As depicted in the previous secIon, it refers to the pracIce of defining the desired state of applicaIons in a declaraIve manner, rather than imperaIvely specifying the steps to achieve that state. There are several benefits to using a declaraIve approach with the Kubernetes API:

• Desired State Management: DeclaraIve APIs enable specifying what the system is expected to look like (the desired state) rather than how to get there (the imperaIve steps). Kubernetes controllers conInuously work to reconcile the current state with the desired state, automaIcally making adjustments as needed. This simplifies operaIons of keeping resources in sync with the intenIon and reduces the risk of configuraIon driC.
  • Resilient: DeclaraIve object configuraIon enables Kubernetes to automaIcally detect and recover from failures. If a pod or other resource goes down or becomes unhealthy, Kubernetes will automaIcally create a new instance to maintain the desired state.
  • Idempotence: In a declaraIve API, applying the same configuraIon mulIple Imes have the same result as applying it once. This idempotence property reduces the risk of unexpected changes or side effects when managing resources.
  • Scalability: Objects created declaraIvely are oCen easier to scale because mulIple instances of the same resource using the same configuraIon template can be defined. Kubernetes can then create and manage these instances as needed.

• Version Control and AudiBng: DeclaraIve configuraIons can be stored in version control systems like Git [11], allowing for versioning, history tracking, and easy collaboraIon. This helps with audiIng and troubleshooIng as the evoluIon of the configuraIon is visible over Ime.
  • Predictable Rollouts and Rollbacks: With declaraIve APIs, a new desired state can be specified, and Kubernetes will manage the rollout and rollback of resources to achieve that state. This makes it easier to perform updates and handle failures gracefully.
  • Portability: DeclaraIve configuraIons are oCen agnosIc to the underlying infrastructure, making it easier to move workloads between different Kubernetes clusters or cloud providers. If the declaraIve configuraIons embed some details that are specific to some environments, then the portability becomes limited to these environments.
  • AutomaBon and Tooling: DeclaraIve APIs are well-suited for automaIon because configuraIon is defined as code enabling the use of tools like Helm [10], Kustomize [12], or operators to manage complex applicaIons and resources.
  • Human-Readable: DeclaraIve configuraIons are oCen more human-readable and maintainable compared to imperaIve scripts or instrucIons, which can be error-prone and hard to understand.

In summary, the declaraIve nature of the Kubernetes API simplifies resource management, enhances automaIon, increase reliability, and makes it easier to work with complex infrastructure and applicaIons in a dynamic environment like Kubernetes.
NOTE: The present document only assesses Kubernetes technology; it can be possible to realize these benefits with other technologies as well.
4.3.3 Industry Adoption

As highlighted in the CNCF Cloud NaIve DefiniIon v1.0 [5], the adopIon of declaraIve APIs empowers organizaIons to develop and operate scalable applicaIons in modern and dynamic environments, introducing GitOps as a new approach for managing the operaIon and the lifecycle of telecom networks. But transiIoning to GitOps can be challenging due to potenIal cultural shiCs and skillset gaps.
At its core, GitOps principles encompass the following [6]:

• DeclaraBve: A system managed using GitOps expresses its desired state in a declaraIve manner.
  • Versioned and Immutable: The desired state of a system is stored in a manner that enforces immutability, versioning, and maintains a complete version history.
  • AutomaBcally Pulled: SoCware agents automaIcally retrieve the desired state declaraIons from the source.
• ConBnuously Reconciled: SoCware agents consistently monitor the actual system state and strive to apply the desired state.

The Cloud-NaIve Telco Market PercepIon Report [4] sIpulates wanIng "to know which technologies and companies are perceived by the network operator community to be important to cloud-naIve telco strategies – so [their report] is all about percepIon, not which technologies and companies are actually involved with, or linked to, any cloud-naIve developments at the network operators represented by our survey respondents.". 4.4 O2-IMS Services Analysis
4.4.1 Introduction

As of specificaIon v04.00, the O2-IMS interface is composed of services at various stages of standardizaIon. This secIon analyses each O2 IMS service, along with its applicability to a declaraIve interface.
4.4.2 Inventory Service
This service enables querying the O-Cloud resources and management services.

The inventory service defines objects which are exposed as read-only to the SMO. The only REST resource method supported is "GET", except for the SubscripIon object which also supports "POST" and "DELETE".
As part of the "GET" resource methods, a comprehensive list of query parameters is defined.

It is technically possible to implement an inventory system with the O2 IMS Inventory objects defined as Kubernetes Custom Resource DefiniIons (CRDs), but there are certain consideraIons and challenges that can make this approach less desirable:

• Scalability and Performance: CRDs can introduce performance overhead, especially when dealing with a large number of objects. Kubernetes itself is primarily designed for managing infrastructure and applicaIon workloads, and using it for inventory management might not be as efficient as purpose-built inventory systems.
  • Complexity: Managing inventory typically involves complex data structures and relaIonships. CRDs might not provide the necessary data modeling and querying capabiliIes needed for complex inventory structures, which could lead to a more complex and less efficient inventory management system.
  • Lack of Inventory-Specific Features: Kubernetes CRDs are not designed specifically for inventory management. They lack features such as built-in reporIng, audiIng, and advanced querying capabiliIes that are oCen essenIal for inventory systems.

• Data Consistency: Ensuring data consistency and integrity in an inventory system is criIcal. CRDs do not inherently enforce data consistency rules or provide transacIonal guarantees, which might be necessary for inventory systems with stringent data requirements.
  • Limited Control over Data Storage: Kubernetes abstracts much of the underlying infrastructure, including data storage. In some cases, it can be needed to have more control over how inventory data is stored, indexed, and retrieved than what CRDs offer.
  • MigraBon and Portability: It can be challenging to extract and convert data from Kubernetes CRDs when the inventory system needs to migrate to a different platorm or infrastructure.

Kubernetes CRDs provide flexibility and extensibility for managing custom resources within a Kubernetes cluster, they might not be the best choice for implemenIng a complex inventory management system. It can be more pracIcal to use purpose-built inventory management tools or databases that are designed to handle the complexiIes and challenges associated with inventory management.
4.4.3 Provisioning Service

Provisioning clusters declaraIvely through CRDs can offer several advantages, especially in scenarios where a high degree of automaIon, customizaIon, and control over cluster deployments is expected. Some of the advantages are:

• Infrastructure as Code (IaC): DeclaraIve provisioning with CRDs enables defining the cluster lifecycle management operaIons as code. This means the cluster configuraIon can be versioned, reviewed, and managed using familiar development pracIces, making it easier to track changes and collaborate with others.
  • AutomaBon: CRDs enable automaIon of cluster provisioning. By defining the cluster's desired state in CRDs, tools like Kubernetes Operators or custom controllers can be used to automaIcally reconcile the actual state with the desired state, reducing manual intervenIon and potenIal human error.
  • CustomizaBon: Kubernetes CRDs enable customizaIon of the cluster's configuraIon to the specific needs. Custom resource types to represent different types of clusters (e.g., development, producIon, tesIng) and configure them with disInct sevngs, such as node sizes, networking opIons, and addons, can be defined.
  • Reusability: CRD definiIons can be reused and shared across different infrastructures or environments. This can lead to consistent cluster configuraIons and simplify the management of mulIple clusters with similar requirements.

• Versioning and Rollbacks: CRD-based configuraIons are versioned, making it straightorward to roll back to previous cluster configuraIons if issues arise during an update. This provides a safety net for changes to the cluster infrastructure.
  • Ecosystem IntegraBon: Using CRDs aligns the cluster provisioning process with KubernetesnaIve concepts, making it easier to integrate with other Kubernetes components and tools in the ecosystem. This includes monitoring, logging, and scaling soluIons designed to work seamlessly with Kubernetes.
  • Scalability: As the needs change, scaling clusters up or down is achieved by updaIng the CRD instance configuraIons. This flexibility ensures the clusters can adapt to evolving workloads and resource requirements.
  • ConBnuous IntegraBon/ConBnuous Deployment (CI/CD): DeclaraIve cluster provisioning fits seamlessly into CI/CD pipelines by automaIng cluster creaIon as part of the deployment process, ensuring clusters are always up to date with the latest configuraIons.

DeclaraIve provisioning of clusters through CRDs offers a powerful way to automate, customize, and manage clusters efficiently. It aligns well with Kubernetes principles and best pracIces, making it a compelling choice for organizaIons seeking greater control and automaIon over their cluster infrastructure.

It is inline with the goal of the present document of adopIng a declaraIve API approach for the provisioning service. And this is inline with the goal of having a declaraIve way to manage lifecycle events of O-Cloud Node Clusters.

4.4.6 Monitoring Service

Kubernetes CRDs offer a flexible way to extend the Kubernetes API and define custom resources, but they might not be the most suitable choice for implemenIng a monitoring service for metrics, faults, and alarms for the following reasons:

• Performance Overhead: Monitoring systems typically deal with high volumes of data and require low-latency access to metrics and alarms. Storing this data as CRDs within Kubernetes can introduce performance overhead due to the way Kubernetes handles resource storage and retrieval.
  • Data Volume and RetenBon: Monitoring systems oCen generate and store a large amount of Ime-series data.   • Data TransformaBon and Enrichment: Monitoring oCen involves data transformaIon and enrichment processes to make sense of raw metrics and create meaningful dashboards and reports. ImplemenIng these processes within CRDs can be complex and might not be the most efficient approach.
  • Scalability and High Availability: Monitoring services scale horizontally to handle increasing data volumes and ensure high availability. Kubernetes CRDs might not offer the same level of scalability and high availability features as dedicated monitoring soluIons.
  • Ecosystem CompaBbility: The broader monitoring ecosystem, including popular tools like Prometheus, Grafana, and ElasIcsearch, is not naIvely designed to work with Kubernetes CRDs. Using CRDs needs of significant customizaIon and integraIon work.
  • OperaBonal Overhead: Maintaining a monitoring system implemented with CRDs might introduce operaIonal complexity, due to the management and maintenance both the monitoring system and the Kubernetes cluster.

As described, CRDs might not be the best choice for implemenIng a comprehensive monitoring service. Specialized monitoring soluIons are be\er equipped to handle the complexiIes of monitoring, alerIng, data storage, querying, and integraIon with external systems and data
sources, while also providing the necessary performance and scalability required for monitoring large-scale and criIcal applicaIons.

4.5.2 URI compatibility

In Kubernetes, CRDs are accessed and managed through the Kubernetes API server, which listens on the following URI endpoint: /apis/{group}/{version}/{resource}. More details on Kubernetes Resource URIs can be found in its documentaIon [7].
An URI endpoint is comprised of the following parts:

• {group}: The API group to which the CRD belongs. Custom resources are oCen grouped under a specific API group to avoid naming conflicts with built-in resources. For example, the group of a CRD for a custom applicaIon can be myapp.example.com.
  • {version}: The version of the CRD. As the CRD evolves, there can create mulIple versions to handle changes in the resource definiIon. For example, version can be v1alpha1, v1beta1, or v1.
  • {resource}: The name of the custom resource. This is typically pluralized. For example, if the custom resource is called MyApp, the resource name might be myapps.
The K8s URI endpoint structure is inline with the currently defined O2 IMS URI structure, defined in secIon 3.1.2 in v04.00: {apiRoot}/<apiName>/<apiMajorVersion>/<apiSpecificResourceUriPart>

In order to support both a RESTful interface and Kubernetes API for the O2 IMS Provisioning service, the proposal is:

• Ensure the {apiName} comply to a lowercase RFC 1123 subdomain, secIon 2.1 "Host Names and Numbers" which limits host names to le\ers-digits-hyphen.

  • Have two data models; one being a JSON document, and one being in the format of CRD(s).
